picks.why: A single pot still label first bottled by the Dublin merchants W. and A. Gilbey from Jameson's Bow Street spirit, taken on by Irish Distillers in 1986 and relaunched as a twelve year old in 1991. Distilled at Midleton from malted and unmalted barley in copper pot stills and matured in ex-bourbon and oloroso sherry casks, bottled at 40% ABV, it is the bottle that shows a guest what Irish pot still tastes like.
picks.note: Sources split on the label's start, about 1903 or 1912: tell it as the early twentieth century, or leave the year out. The Library's Midleton record holds the distillery that makes it; the Library has no Redbreast record of its own. Keep the robin nickname story out unless two sources agree on it.

picks.madeBy: Midleton Distillery, for Mitchell & Son of Dublin
picks.why: A bonder's label of the Dublin wine merchant Mitchell & Son, named for the daub of paint that once marked the age of a cask in its cellars, and made for it at Midleton. Bottled without an age statement at 40% ABV from young pot still whiskey, it is the pot still that kept the style alive in the years when Redbreast was off the market.
picks.note: Sources split on when the Spot names began (the 1887 bonding trade or the 1920s): tell it as the early twentieth century. Yellow Spot, Red Spot and Blue Spot are the same label and stay out of every other group. Confirm the cask make up (sources give 7 to 10 year old pot still, some sherry casks).

picks.flagship: Powers John's Lane Release 12 Year Old
picks.why: The Dublin name begun by James Power in 1791, whose John's Lane distillery closed in 1976 when its spirit moved to the new Midleton site. John's Lane Release is single pot still aged at least twelve years, mainly in ex-bourbon casks with a little oloroso, bottled at 46% ABV without chill filtering: the spicier, oilier Dublin answer to Redbreast.
picks.note: Powers Gold Label, the blend an Irish pub pours, belongs to this same label and is held here; it is kept out of the blended group so that the label is used once. Confirm 1791 against the brand's pages (one source only). John's Lane is told in the past tense.

picks.why: Teeling opened its distillery at Newmarket in Dublin in 2015, and its single pot still, distilled there that year from an even split of malted and unmalted barley and bottled at 46% ABV, was the first new Dublin distilled Irish whiskey in some fifty years. It is the bottle that shows pot still from a house outside Midleton.
picks.note: Teeling Small Batch (a blend) and Teeling Single Grain belong to this label and stay here; that is why the Irish single grain group is left. Sources differ on the casks (virgin oak, ex-bourbon and ex-wine in the launch material): use the producer's own list. Keep the family's living members out of prose.

picks.why: An independent distillery on the Kerry coast whose first casks were filled in December 2012; in 2017 it became the first independent Irish distillery in decades to release a single pot still. Its core Single Pot Still, made from local malted and unmalted barley, is the craft counterpoint to the Midleton houses.
picks.note: Dingle stands in the single malt benchmarks too; it is placed here, where its newer core bottling teaches the style, and is kept out of the single malt group. Confirm the core strength on the label (one source gives 46.5% ABV for the 2017 batch). Oliver Hughes (dead) may be named as a co-founder; his living co-founders are kept out of prose.

alternates.why: Double distilled in copper pot stills at Kilbeggan in County Westmeath from malted and unmalted barley with a little oats, after a late nineteenth century recipe, and bottled at 43% ABV.

alternates.flagship: Method and Madness Single Pot Still
alternates.why: The experimental label of Irish Distillers, made at Midleton; confirm the current single pot still bottling and its finish before use.

picks.why: The Antrim distillery whose label carries 1608, the year of a royal licence to distil in the county; the distillery company itself was registered in 1784. Its ten year old is triple distilled from malted barley alone and matured in bourbon and oloroso casks, bottled at 40% ABV: the reference for the soft, triple distilled Irish malt.
picks.note: Tell 1608 as the licence and 1784 as the company, never 1608 as the distillery. Bushmills Original and Black Bush, the blends, belong to this label and are held here, so Bushmills stays out of the blended group. Sources differ on the malts in the ten (10 to 12 years).

picks.why: Cooley's peated single malt, double rather than triple distilled, which revives the old Irish habit of drying barley over peat fires. It is the bottle to reach for when a guest asks whether Ireland makes a smoky whiskey.
picks.note: Confirm the launch year (the 1990s) and the strength on the current label (40% ABV in the sources). The peat is now sourced from Scotland: say so only if the author confirms it on the producer's pages.

picks.why: A Derry name of the Watt family, whose distillery closed in 1925, revived by the newly formed Cooley Distillery in 1993 as a pot still single malt. Named for a family racehorse, it is the unpeated Cooley malt to set beside Connemara.
picks.note: Sources split on 1762 (the Watt merchant business or the distillery) and on the year the horse won: leave both out or tell them as the family's story. The Watt distillery is told in the past tense. Confirm the current core bottling (age statement or none) and its strength.

picks.madeBy: Sourced; the triple distillation points to Bushmills
picks.why: A label named for a castle in County Clare, sold as a triple distilled single malt from malted barley, aged twelve years in bourbon casks. It is the twelve year old a bar meets most often after Bushmills, and it teaches that many Irish malt labels are bottled from another house's stills.
picks.note: In doubt. The distillery is not stated by the producer: say only that it is sourced. Strength differs by listing (40%, 43% and 46% ABV): confirm on the current label. Replace with an alternate if the author cannot confirm the bottling is current.

picks.why: The single malt of Walsh Whiskey, a Carlow house founded in 1999, sold as one of a handful of triple distilled Irish single malts. It sits beside Writers' Tears from the same house and shows a malt made to be poured neat.
picks.note: In doubt. The Library and the style's benchmarks do not name it; confirm the current core bottling (no age statement, and its strength) and where it is distilled (Walsh first contracted its spirit out). The founders are living and stay out of prose. Dingle, a benchmark of this style, is placed in single pot still instead.

alternates.why: Waterford's core single malt, built from single farm origin whiskeys of Irish grown barley; confirm the distillery's present state before use, as it went into receivership in late 2024.
A Wicklow craft house better known for its single grain; confirm the current single malt bottling before use.

picks.why: The name of John Jameson, a Scot who had his Bow Street distillery in Dublin running by 1780; its whiskey moved to Midleton in the 1970s. Today a blend of grain whiskey and single pot still, triple distilled and bottled at 40% ABV, it is the Irish whiskey a guest asks for by name and the usual whiskey of the Irish Coffee.
picks.note: Sources split on the last Bow Street distillation (1970 or 1975): tell it as the 1970s. Bow Street is told in the past tense as a distillery; its 18 year old finish there is a later bottling, not a return of distilling. The Library's Midleton record holds the distillery.

picks.why: A blend from Tullamore in County Offaly, traced to 1829 and named for the initials of Daniel E. Williams, who rose from the stables to run the distillery. The Original is a triple blend of grain, malt and pot still whiskey at 40% ABV, and distilling returned to the town when a new distillery opened in 2014.
picks.note: The town's first distillery closed in 1954: tell it in the past tense. Sources split on its builders (the Molloy brothers): leave them out. The brand's own claims about being the only one of its kind are marketing and stay out.

picks.why: A Walsh Whiskey blend with no grain whiskey at all: aged single pot still married to single malt, from malted and unmalted barley, bottled at 40% ABV. It teaches that an Irish blend can be a marriage of the two pot still styles.
picks.note: Where it is distilled is not disclosed: say that it is sourced. The Walsh founders are living and stay out of prose. The Irishman, from the same house, is a separate label in the single malt group.

picks.madeBy: Midleton Distillery, for the Sazerac Company
picks.why: The Cork Distilleries Company's old Irish whiskey, renamed for Paddy Flaherty, the salesman who carried it round the pubs of Cork. A triple distilled blend of pot still, malt and grain, made at Midleton for Sazerac since a sale agreed in 2016, it is the Cork pour to set beside Jameson.
picks.note: Sources split on the renaming (1912 or 1913) and on when Flaherty joined (1881 or 1882): tell it as the early twentieth century. Confirm the label strength (40% ABV).

picks.why: Made in the old stables of Slane Castle in County Meath, a distillery Brown-Forman built after buying the brand in 2015, and launched in 2017. It is a blend aged in virgin oak, seasoned American whiskey barrels and oloroso sherry casks, bottled at 40% ABV, and shows a new house teaching cask influence on a blend.
picks.note: Early releases used bought in whiskey: say that the blend now draws on the castle's own stills only if the author confirms it. The castle's family are living and stay out of prose. Powers is held in the single pot still group although its Gold Label is a blend; Bushmills likewise in single malt.

alternates.why: Diageo's blend of malt and grain whiskey at 45% ABV, launched in 2017 and named for George Roe, whose Thomas Street distillery in Dublin is long closed; a new distillery near the old site began production in 2019.

alternates.flagship: The Busker Irish Whiskey Triple Cask Triple Smooth
alternates.why: A blend from the Royal Oak Distillery in County Carlow; confirm the label and its strength before use.

picks.why: Japan's first malt whisky distillery, founded near Kyoto by Shinjiro Torii in 1923. The twelve year old came out in 1984, labelled a pure malt until 2004, as the first single malt Japan marketed in earnest; at 43% ABV it is the bottle a guest means by Japanese single malt.
picks.note: Keizo Saji (dead) may be named as the founder's son behind the 1984 release. Suntory's living blenders stay out of prose. Confirm the label wording for the market (Suntory Whisky The Yamazaki).

picks.why: Suntory's second malt distillery, built in 1973 in the forests of the Southern Alps in Yamanashi, at about 700 metres. Its twelve year old, gently smoky and herbal at 43% ABV, is the green, mountain counterpoint to Yamazaki.
picks.note: Some listings give 43.5% ABV: confirm on the label. Describe the peat as gentle and say it varies by batch; do not call it a peated whisky.

picks.why: Nikka's first distillery, built in 1934 on the Hokkaido coast by Masataka Taketsuru, and still distilling over direct coal fire. Its single malt, bottled at 45% ABV, is the heavier, sea air malt every Japanese course sets beside the Suntory pair.
picks.note: The age statements were withdrawn in 2015; a Yoichi 10 Years Old returned in 2022. Confirm whether the author teaches the no age statement bottling or the ten. The distillery was named an Important Cultural Property in 2021.

picks.why: Nikka's second distillery, built in 1969 in the hills of Miyagi, which makes a softer, fruitier malt than Yoichi. Its single malt at 45% ABV lets a guest taste the two Nikka houses side by side.
picks.note: Miyagikyo 10 Years Old returned in July 2026, its first age statement since 2015: confirm which bottling the author teaches. Confirm the still type before writing about it (the sources do not).

picks.why: Hombo Shuzo's distillery in Nagano, established in 1985 as Mars Shinshu with stills moved from Yamanashi, silent after 1992 and reopened in 2011; it now carries the name Komagatake. Single Malt Komagatake is the flagship of its range, and shows a Japanese malt house beyond the two large firms.
picks.note: In doubt on the label wording: the producer launched Single Malt KOMAGATAKE as its flagship in 2025; confirm the name as printed and the strength. Sources split on 1984 or 1985 for the move: use 1985 from the producer's pages. The benchmark lists it as Mars Shinshu.

alternates.why: The Saitama distillery licensed in 2008; The First Ten, released in 2020 at 50.5% ABV, was its first ten year old. Its other labels carry its living founder's own name, which stays out of prose.
A Kagoshima malt distillery of a shochu family, opened in 2017; confirm the current core bottling and strength before use.

groups.title: Japanese blended whisky and the highball

picks.why: Created in 1937 by Shinjiro Torii and named for its square, tortoiseshell cut bottle, a 40% ABV blend drawing on Yamazaki, Hakushu and Chita. It is the whisky of the Kaku highball, the drink that put the Japanese highball on bar menus, and the first blend to learn.
picks.note: Sources call it Kakubin, Kaku and Yellow Label: use the label's own wording. Suntory's sales claims stay out.

picks.why: Suntory's flagship blend, first launched in 1989; Japanese Harmony followed in 2015, a no age statement blend of malt and grain from Yamazaki, Hakushu and Chita at 43% ABV. It is the Hibiki a bar is likely to pour and the lesson in how Japanese blenders build a blend from their own distilleries.
picks.note: One listing gives 42% ABV: confirm on the label. The aged Hibiki bottlings are not the flagship.

picks.why: A Suntory blend made for the highball, built on Hakushu malt and Chita grain with two Yamazaki malts for depth, bottled at 43% ABV with no age statement. Its name means time, and it is the blend a bar keeps on the rail for highballs.
picks.note: In doubt on the date: the 2016 launch for North America is not confirmed by the searches; leave the year out unless the author confirms it. The blender named in one source is living and stays out of prose.

picks.why: A blend of malt and Coffey grain whiskies, chiefly from Yoichi and Miyagikyo, first released in 1985, married in cask and bottled at 51.4% ABV in a small square bottle. It is the Nikka blend a bartender is asked for and shows that a blend can be strong and dense.
picks.note: The barrel in the name does not mean barrel proof: say so. One source says a little Scotch malt goes in; Nikka's own page says mostly its own malts: confirm before writing about the make up, and check how the Japanese whisky standard is shown on the label. The blender named in one source may be living; keep the name out.

picks.why: A blended malt, malt whisky only, from Yoichi and Miyagikyo with Miyagikyo to the fore, bottled at 43% ABV and named for Masataka Taketsuru, Nikka's founder. It teaches the other kind of blend: two malts married with no grain.
picks.note: It is a blended malt, not a blended whisky: say so in the why's first line on the page. The benchmarks name Taketsuru under japanese-whisky and japanese-single-malt as an also known; it is placed here. Confirm the current bottling is the no age statement Pure Malt.

alternates.why: A Nikka blend of 1962 with a high share of Yoichi and Miyagikyo malt, bottled at 43% ABV; it shares the Nikka house with From the Barrel.
A blend of Eigashima Shuzo in Hyogo; confirm how it stands against the Japanese whisky standard before use.

picks.why: The whisky of Hiram Walker, a grain merchant who founded his business in 1858 and moved his distillery across the river from Detroit to Windsor. The 1858 Original is blended before it is aged and bottled at 40% ABV, and it is the Canadian whisky a guest names in a highball or a Manhattan.
picks.note: One retailer gives six years in oak: confirm the age before stating it. The label is sold by one company and made at Hiram Walker's Windsor distillery by another: say only where it is made.

picks.why: Created by Seagram's Samuel Bronfman for the royal tour of 1939 by King George VI and Queen Elizabeth, and made today only at Gimli on Lake Winnipeg. Fine De Luxe, a blend of some fifty whiskies at 40% ABV in its purple bag, is the Canadian whisky a guest names first.
picks.note: Sources split on Gimli's opening (1968, and 1991 for Crown Royal's move there): leave the year out. Strength confirmed only as 80 US proof: confirm 40% ABV on the label.

picks.why: The label of J.P. Wiser, distilled today at Hiram Walker in Windsor; Deluxe at 40% ABV is the everyday Canadian blend of Ontario and the bottle that teaches Canadian blending of corn and rye whiskies distilled apart.
picks.note: In doubt on the founding: J.P. Wiser and Prescott in 1857 were not confirmed by the searches; leave the year out unless the author confirms it. Keep the company that sells it out of prose.

picks.why: A distillery in Grimsby between Hamilton and Niagara Falls whose whiskies of corn, rye and barley are distilled and aged apart and then blended; Barrel Select at 40% ABV is its main bottling. It is the Canadian whisky behind many an Old Pal and shows the newer Ontario school.
picks.note: The founder is living and stays out of prose. Sources differ on the order of the grains: list them without order. The sale to Campari is volatile talk and stays out.

picks.why: A whisky of unmalted rye alone, distilled in a single copper pot still at Hiram Walker in Windsor and bottled at 43% ABV, named for the plot where Joshua Booth ran his first pot still. It is the rye a bartender reaches for to show what Canadian rye means when it is all rye.
picks.note: The master blender is living and stays out of prose. Confirm the cask (new charred American oak in one source) before stating it.

alternates.why: A Toronto name of the nineteenth century revived as a four grain Canadian blend made at Hiram Walker in Windsor; confirm the current label and strength before use. Alberta Distillers' 100% rye from Calgary is the other choice, but its label name carries a word the house voice refuses.
An old Seagram Canadian blend; confirm the current label, its maker and its strength before use.

picks.madeBy: King Car Group, Yuanshan, Yilan County, Taiwan
picks.why: Taiwan's single malt house in Yilan County, whose first new make ran on 11 March 2006; the Classic, released in December 2008 at 40% ABV and matured mainly in American oak, was its first bottling. It is the bottle that teaches how heat and humidity speed maturation.
picks.note: Sources split on the distillery's founding (2005 or 2006): use 2006 for the first spirit. The Cask Atlas chapter names Kavalan already.

picks.why: An Indian single malt from Bengaluru, made from Indian six row barley with a quarter peated Scottish barley, bottled at 50% ABV without chill filtering. Fusion is the bottle that shows how a hot climate gives a young malt depth.
picks.note: Confirm the barley share and the age on the producer's pages (one tasting site gives four and a half years). Keep the family's living members out of prose. Paul John, named in the Cask Atlas chapter, is left out because the label is a living person's name.

picks.why: A Melbourne distillery whose signature single malt, Nova, is matured entirely in Australian red wine barrels filled while still wet and bottled at 41% ABV. It is the Australian malt a bar is likely to carry and teaches the wine cask as house style.
picks.note: The founder is living and stays out of prose. Confirm the age (two years in the sources) before stating it.

picks.flagship: Sullivans Cove French Oak Single Cask
picks.why: A Hobart distillery founded in 1994, distilling from 1995, whose single malts are bottled one cask at a time, usually at 47.5% ABV. The French Oak single cask, from ex-tawny casks, is the bottle that teaches Tasmanian malt, one cask at a time.
picks.note: Strength and age vary by cask: give neither as fixed. Award talk stays out. The Cask Atlas chapter asks that Tasmania be told apart from the mainland.

picks.why: The Welsh distillery that first ran spirit in September 2000 and released its first single malt on St David's Day 2004. Its Madeira Finish, matured in bourbon barrels and finished in Madeira casks, bottled at 46% ABV, is the house style and the world whisky from closest to Scotland.
picks.note: In doubt as to the group: Wales sits outside the chapter's four journeys (Taiwan, India, Australia, New Zealand). Keep it here as elsewhere, or swap in Cardrona for New Zealand if the author wants the chapter's four countries. Confirm the current label name (some markets print Madeira).

alternates.why: The Hobart distillery that began Tasmania's modern whisky; the Cask Atlas chapter cites it as a source. Confirm the current core bottling before use; its founder is living.
A Central Otago distillery named in the Cask Atlas chapter for New Zealand; confirm the current core single malt and its name as printed before use.

left.why: Thin, and the one name a guest asks for is already used. The real single grain labels found are Teeling Single Grain (Cooley grain, red wine casks, 46% ABV), Kilbeggan Single Grain (made at Cooley, mostly corn, 43% ABV), Method and Madness Single Grain (Midleton, 46% ABV) and Glendalough Double Barrel (Coffey still, 42% ABV), with The Busker as a possible fifth. Teeling stands in single pot still and Kilbeggan in its alternates, so the group would be three or four labels of bottlings few guests ask for by name. Teach the style through the label term on its own page.

A standard, not a kind of producer: the makers' association rule of 2021 (malted grain and Japanese water, distilled, aged at least three years and bottled in Japan) covers malts, grain and blends alike. Its houses are carried by japanese-single-malt and japanese-blended.

A wood, not a kind of producer. No five bottlings are asked for by name with Mizunara as their identity; the benchmarks (Yamazaki, Chivas Regal, Bowmore) use it as a finish or a limited release. Teach it on its page through those houses.
